title: Writing on the forehead
hook: a receipt in a coat pocket, a record no one else can read: the Oankar on what is written, and Japji on the deeds that write it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gurmukh's learning: learning that turns over one line until it opens. Your line was reflect. Which line did you turn over, and did it give anything back? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

A coat comes out of the closet after a long summer, and in the pocket there's a receipt. Coffee for two, a date, a time. It's faded, but it's still there. Nobody meant to keep it. It just stayed, a small record of something that actually happened. There's an old way of speaking about the record of a life: what's written on the forehead. The Oankar, Guru Nanak's alphabet poem in Raga Ramkali, picks up that old picture of writing. So does the Japji. Put the two side by side and a question comes up. Who holds the pen?
screen: `A RECEIPT IN AN OLD COAT.` → `WHAT'S WRITTEN ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `WHO HOLDS THE PEN?`

segments.voice: Start with the Oankar. In one of its stanzas, Guru Nanak speaks to a friend, sakhi, and says, in paraphrase: the writing does not get erased, the writing the Creator has written. What is written cannot be turned back; as it pleases You, so take care of it. The word for that writing is lekh. On its own, that could sound like a locked door. Everything decided, nothing to do. But keep reading. The same stanza ends, in paraphrase: by Your glance of grace, peace is found, reflecting on the Word. The writing is not the whole story. Grace is in the room. Now turn to the Japji, on ang four. There Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: being called virtuous or sinful is not just talk. The actions you do, again and again, are written down, and you carry them with you. You sow, and you eat what you sow. Here the pen is in our own hand. Not one big deed, but karna, doing, repeated, until it becomes the record. So the scripture holds three things together: the Creator's writing, our own deeds writing day after day, and grace that can arrive. Sikh readers explain how these fit in more than one way, and this path won't settle it for them. But the picture is clear enough for a Tuesday. A record is being kept, and part of it is being written right now, by what we actually do. Not by what we meant. Not by what we said we'd do. The receipt in the coat pocket was printed by a real afternoon. So what will today's line on the forehead say? Today's line: what's written.
screen: `THE WRITING IS NOT ERASED.` · `GRACE IS IN THE ROOM.` · `DEEDS, REPEATED, ARE WRITTEN DOWN.` · `PART OF IT IS WRITTEN TODAY.` · then, large: `WHAT'S WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one good deed, and do it on purpose. Sit for a moment first. Let one person come to mind who could use something small from you today: a message, a ride, a meal, a thank-you, an hour of help. Pick one. Make it plain enough to finish before tonight. Now see yourself doing it, start to end. Then rest with the breath for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. If you don't, let the choice settle quietly, like ink drying. The bell holds the time.
Writing on the forehead. The lekh, the record of a life: in the Oankar, the Creator's writing; in the Japji, deeds done again and again, written down and carried. Today's word.
Your line: what's written. Do the good deed you chose, all the way through, and tonight notice that it happened. That's one line on today's page. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Sikh teaching, lekh, what is written, is spoken of alongside karam, deeds, and nadar, grace; some teachers present it less as fate to wait out than as a reason for honest work and seva.

what it means: the Oankar speaks of the Creator's writing, and ends the stanza on grace; the Japji says deeds done again and again are written and carried.
what a scholar hears: lekh, karam and nadar, writing, deeds and grace, held together; Sikh readers explain how they fit in more than one way.
